qa.name: Foot Lumbricals (1–4)
qa.origin: Lumbrical 1: medial border of FDL tendon to the second toe. Lumbricals 2–4: adjacent borders of FDL tendons to toes 2–5
qa.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansions of toes 2–5
qa.innervation: Lumbrical 1: medial plantar nerve (L5, S1). Lumbricals 2–4: lateral plantar nerve, deep branch (S1, S2)
qa.function: Flex the MTP joints of toes 2–5; extend the IP joints via the extensor expansions; prevent toe clawing
qa.opposing_muscle: Extensor Digitorum Longus (MTP extension); Flexor Digitorum Longus (IP flexion)
qa.clinical_note: The four foot lumbricals are numbered 1–4 from medial to lateral, arising from the FDL tendons in the second plantar layer. Lumbrical 1 is the only one innervated by the medial plantar nerve (L5–S1); Lumbricals 2–4 are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve (S1–S2). This mirrors the hand where Lumbricals 1–2 are median nerve and 3–4 are ulnar nerve. They flex MTP and extend IP joints — the intrinsic-plus position. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, lumbrical wasting causes clawing of the lesser toes with pressure ulcers under the metatarsal heads.

qa.name: Quadratus Plantae
qa.origin: Two heads: medial head from medial surface of calcaneus; lateral head from lateral border of calcaneus
qa.insertion: Posterolateral border of the FDL tendon before it divides into four slips
qa.function: Straightens the oblique pull of FDL — redirects the FDL tendons to pull in line with the toes rather than obliquely toward the medial leg
qa.clinical_note: Quadratus Plantae (also called Flexor Accessorius) is unique in that its sole purpose is to correct the angle of pull of FDL — FDL pulls obliquely toward the medial leg, and Quadratus Plantae redirects this force to act straight along the toes. It has no bony insertion of its own. It is the only muscle in the second plantar layer that is not a lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve and artery pass between the first and second layers — a key surgical landmark in plantar foot approaches.

qa.name: Lumbrical 1
qa.origin: Medial border of the FDL tendon to the second toe
qa.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansion (dorsal digital expansion) of the second toe
qa.innervation: Medial plantar nerve (L5, S1); first lumbrical only
qa.function: Flexes the MTP joint of the second toe; extends the IP joints of the second toe via the extensor expansion
qa.opposing_muscle: Extensor Digitorum Longus (MTP extension); Flexor Digitorum Longus (IP flexion)
qa.clinical_note: The foot lumbricals mirror the hand lumbricals in origin and action — arising from FDL tendons and inserting into extensor expansions. Lumbrical 1 is the only foot lumbrical innervated by the medial plantar nerve (L5–S1); Lumbricals 2–4 are innervated by the lateral plantar nerve (S1–S2) — the same medial/lateral split as in the hand (median/ulnar nerve). The lumbricals flex the MTP joints and extend the IP joints — preventing clawing of the toes.

qa.name: Lumbrical 2
qa.origin: Adjacent borders of FDL tendons to the second and third toes
qa.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansion of the third toe
qa.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch (S1, S2); second lumbrical — third toe
qa.function: Flexes the MTP joint of the third toe; extends the IP joints of the third toe
qa.opposing_muscle: Extensor Digitorum Longus; Flexor Digitorum Longus
qa.clinical_note: Lumbrical 2 is the first of three lumbricals innervated by the lateral plantar nerve (S1–S2), in contrast to Lumbrical 1 (medial plantar nerve). It arises from two FDL tendons — a bipennate origin shared with Lumbricals 3 and 4. The foot lumbricals are generally smaller and less functionally significant than the hand lumbricals, but still contribute to preventing toe clawing. Morton's neuroma most commonly affects the interdigital nerve between the third and fourth toes — near the passage of the lateral plantar nerve branches.

qa.name: Lumbrical 3
qa.origin: Adjacent borders of FDL tendons to the third and fourth toes
qa.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansion of the fourth toe
qa.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch (S1, S2); third lumbrical — fourth toe
qa.function: Flexes the MTP joint of the fourth toe; extends the IP joints of the fourth toe
qa.opposing_muscle: Extensor Digitorum Longus; Flexor Digitorum Longus
qa.clinical_note: Lumbrical 3 arises from the adjacent borders of the FDL tendons to the third and fourth toes. All four foot lumbricals insert into the extensor expansions on the medial side of their respective toes — acting to flex MTP and extend IP joints, balancing the extrinsic flexor and extensor tendons. In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, lumbrical wasting leads to intrinsic minus deformity — clawing of the lesser toes with MTP hyperextension and IP flexion, causing pressure sores under the metatarsal heads.

qa.name: Lumbrical 4
qa.origin: Adjacent borders of FDL tendons to the fourth and fifth toes
qa.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansion of the fifth toe
qa.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch (S1, S2); fourth lumbrical — fifth toe
qa.function: Flexes the MTP joint of the fifth toe; extends the IP joints of the fifth toe
qa.opposing_muscle: Extensor Digitorum Longus; Flexor Digitorum Longus
qa.clinical_note: Lumbrical 4 is the most lateral lumbrical, acting on the fifth toe. It shares the same innervation (lateral plantar nerve, S1–S2) and action as Lumbricals 2 and 3. The four foot lumbricals number from medial to lateral (1–4), same as in the hand. Innervation summary: Lumbrical 1 — medial plantar nerve; Lumbricals 2, 3, 4 — lateral plantar nerve. This mirrors the hand where Lumbricals 1 and 2 are median nerve and Lumbricals 3 and 4 are ulnar nerve.
